courses.title: Talking to Claude
courses.tagline: Ask a better question, get a better answer — and people will pay you for the answer.
courses.intro: Claude is a helper made of words. It cannot see you, it cannot smell the rain, and it does not know your street — so everything it gives you depends on how well you ask. In this course you will learn to ask like a champion, and by the last module you will have a tiny real shop that makes real money for you.
courses.parentNote: A grown-up holds the Claude account and opens it — Claude's terms are for adults, so the phone stays in your hand while the child does the thinking, the asking and the selling. There is a free tier with usage limits that change over time, so check the current limits before a session and plan short turns; the first two modules need no device at all.

modules.title: Fat Questions and Thin Questions
modules.bigIdea: A thin question gets a thin answer; a fat question gets an answer you can use.

seeThis.caption: A thin leaf of a question gives you a yawn. A fat loaf of a question gives you something to eat.

youNeed: a friend or a sister or a brother
doThis: Fold your paper down the middle. Write THIN on the left side and FAT on the right side.
On the THIN side write: 'Tell me about goats.' On the FAT side write: 'My goat will not eat this morning. She is one year old. What three things should I check first?' Read both out loud.
Now go and ask a real person the thin one, then the fat one. Count how many words each answer had. Write the two numbers down.
Write five thin questions about things near your house — the maize, the borehole, a football, a kombi, your school.
Turn every one of those five into a fat question by adding WHO, WHERE and HOW MANY. Read your five fat questions to somebody. That page is the thing you made today.
Draw a star next to the fattest question on your page.
modules.whyItWorks: Claude, like a person, can only answer with what you put in front of it. When you say who you are, where you are and how many, you have given it the corners of the picture and it can fill in the middle. A thin question makes it guess, and a guess is where wrong answers are born.
modules.challenge: Ask your grandmother one fat question about her childhood. Listen without interrupting. See how long the answer runs.

words.means: the question or instruction you give the AI
the small extra facts that make an answer fit your real life

modules.title: The Complaint Walk
modules.bigIdea: Every time somebody sighs and says 'ehh, this thing', a small business is hiding there.

seeThis.caption: A complaint becomes a note, a note becomes an idea, an idea becomes a coin.

youNeed: one hour outside with a grown-up's permission
doThis: Walk to the market, the church yard, the kombi stop or the borehole queue. Take your paper.

Listen. Every time somebody complains about something, write it down in their own words. Get ten complaints. 'The prices board is faded.' 'Nobody can read my sign.' 'My daughter's homework defeats me.'
Beside each complaint write WHO said it. A trader? A mother? A driver? A teacher?
Circle the three complaints you heard more than once. Repeat means many people, and many people means customers.
On a fresh page draw one big face — your customer. Write their name, what they sell or do, and the one thing that annoys them. Pin this face on your wall. This is who your shop will serve.
Show the face to a grown-up and say out loud: 'This is my customer.'
modules.whyItWorks: Businesses that fail usually start with 'what do I like making?' Businesses that live start with 'what is annoying people right here?' You cannot invent a complaint from your bedroom — you have to go where people are and let them tell you. Ten complaints on paper is real research, and you did it with no phone and no money.
modules.challenge: Find one complaint that costs somebody money every single week. Those are the best ones.

words.means: the person who will pay you, not the person who likes you
the annoying thing your customer would pay to make go away

modules.title: Your Grown-Up Opens It, You Do the Thinking
modules.bigIdea: The phone belongs to your grown-up; the questions belong to you.

seeThis.caption: Their account, their phone, your brain. That is the team.

youNeed: a grown-up who has opened a Claude account
doThis: Before you touch the phone, write your first prompt on paper. Use module one: who, where, how many.
Ask your grown-up to open Claude and check today's usage limits, because the free tier has limits and they change. Agree how many turns you get today. Ten is plenty.
Read your written prompt out loud, then type it exactly. Do not add extra words while typing.
Read the answer slowly. Underline on your paper the parts that are actually useful to you.
Type one follow-up: 'Make that shorter and use words a nine-year-old knows.' Read the new answer. Notice it changed because you asked.
Copy the best three lines of the answer onto your paper by hand. Now you own them even when the phone goes away.
modules.whyItWorks: Claude's rules say the account belongs to an adult, so your grown-up stays the driver. That is not a punishment — it means somebody is beside you when an answer looks strange. Writing prompts on paper first also saves turns, and on a shared phone with limits, saved turns are saved money.
modules.challenge: Get a useful answer in one single prompt, with no follow-ups. Harder than it sounds.

words.means: the grown-up's login that Claude belongs to
one question and one answer

modules.title: Say It Again, But Simpler
modules.bigIdea: If you do not understand the answer, the answer is not finished yet.

seeThis.caption: The same idea, squeezed smaller and smaller until it fits in your head.

doThis: Ask Claude to explain something hard: why maize prices go up before harvest, or why load-shedding happens.
When the answer is too big, type: 'Explain it again like I am seven. Five sentences only.'
Then type: 'Now explain it in Swahili' — or Shona, Yoruba, Hausa, Amharic, whichever your family speaks at home.
Read the home-language version to somebody who does not read English well. Ask them: did that make sense? Write down exactly what they say.
Write the final five sentences on paper in your best handwriting. That page is a thing you can show anyone.
Ask Claude for one drawing idea to go with your five sentences, then draw it yourself with the pencil.
modules.whyItWorks: Claude can shrink an idea, swap the language, or change who it is speaking to — but only if you tell it to. This is the skill that turns you into a bridge: information arrives in big English, and you hand it to your neighbour in the language they dream in. Bridges get paid.
modules.challenge: Explain your five sentences to a younger child with no paper at all, just your mouth.

words.means: say the same thing in another language
the person the words are for

modules.title: Claude Can Be Wrong
modules.bigIdea: Claude sounds confident even when it is mistaken, so you check before you repeat.

seeThis.caption: Every answer walks past your own eyes before it walks out of your mouth.

youNeed: one person who really knows something
doThis: Ask Claude something you already know the true answer to — the name of your headmaster's school, the price of a loaf at your shop, the date of your own market day.
Write down what Claude said. Then write down what is actually true. Are they the same?
Ask Claude something about your village. Then go and ask a real elder or trader the same thing. Write both answers side by side.
Draw a big CHECK BOX on your wall page and write inside it: 'Did I check this with a real person?'

Now the honesty rules. Copy these three lines onto your page: I never type other people's private things into Claude. I tell my customer when Claude helped me. I never hand in Claude's writing at school as mine.
Read those three lines out loud to your grown-up. They must hear you say them.
modules.whyItWorks: Claude builds sentences that sound right, and sounding right is not the same as being right — especially about your own village, today's prices, or anybody's name. Checking with a real person costs you two minutes and saves your reputation. In a small place, your reputation is the whole business.
modules.challenge: Catch Claude in one honest mistake this week and write it in your book like a hunter's trophy.

words.means: find out from a real person or a real place whether it is true
somebody else's business that is not yours to type anywhere

modules.title: Building the Thing You Will Sell
modules.bigIdea: Your shop sells one small thing done well, not everything done badly.

seeThis.caption: Four ideas go in. One idea comes out — the one you will actually make.

doThis: Take the customer face from module two. Pick ONE thing you could make for them with a pencil, paper and Claude's words. Signs for market stalls. Birthday cards. A neat price list. Labels for jars.
Tell Claude who your customer is and what you will make, then ask: 'Give me six short lines I could write on a market sign for a tomato seller.' Choose the two you like.
Ask Claude to check your spelling in English and in your home language. Fix what is wrong.
Now make it by hand. Draw the sign, the card, the list. Neat lines, big letters, real colour. This is your sample.
Show the sample to three people. Ask: 'Would you want this?' Write down all three answers, even the rude ones.
Make version two, better, using what those three people said.
modules.whyItWorks: Claude is good at words and options, but it cannot hold a pencil or hand a card to your auntie — that part is yours, and that is the part people pay for. Making one sample and showing it to three humans is how real businesses test an idea before spending anything.
modules.challenge: Make your sample so good that one of the three people asks to keep it.

words.means: one finished example you show people before they buy
what people honestly tell you about your work

modules.title: What Will You Charge?
modules.bigIdea: The price must cover what you spent, pay you for your time, and still feel fair to your customer.

seeThis.caption: Two things go into a price. Never forget the second one.

doThis: Write down everything one sign or one card costs you: the paper, the pen, the walk to the printing shop if you use one. Add it up. That is your cost.
Write how long one takes you. Half an hour? Decide what your half hour is worth — small, but not nothing.
Add the two together. Look at the number. Ask three grown-ups: 'Would you pay this?' Adjust once, then stop adjusting.
Practise saying it out loud in the mirror: 'One sign is [your price]. I can have it ready tomorrow.' No mumbling, no apologising.
Ask Claude to help you write a five-line WhatsApp message announcing your shop. Read it aloud. If it does not sound like you, rewrite it in your own words.
Write your price on a card and put it in your pocket. It goes with you everywhere now.
modules.whyItWorks: Children usually price at zero because saying a number feels rude. But free work teaches customers that your work is worth nothing, and then they never pay. A price you can say without flinching is a skill you practise like a song. Some kids selling signs or cards earn a few dollars a week — small, real, and honestly yours.
modules.challenge: Say your price to a stranger without looking at your feet.

words.means: the money you spend to make one thing
the money the customer gives you for it

modules.title: Opening Day
modules.bigIdea: Today you stop practising and serve one real customer for real money.

seeThis.caption: Your record sheet: five columns drawn by hand, one line per customer.

doThis: Rule five columns on a fresh page: DATE, WHO, WHAT I MADE, MONEY IN, DONE. This is your record sheet. Keep it in one place, never loose.
Go to the customer from your complaint walk. Show your sample. Say your price the way you practised.
If they say yes, write the line in your record sheet BEFORE you start working. If they say no, ask why, write that down too, and go to the next person.
Make the thing properly. Deliver it by hand. When you hand it over, say plainly: 'I used an AI helper for the words and I drew it myself.' Honest sellers get sent more customers.
Take the money in front of your grown-up, or into their mobile money, and write it in the MONEY IN column. Tick DONE.
Split what you earned into three piles on the table: one to buy more paper and pens, one to save, one small pile for you. Draw the three piles at the bottom of your record sheet.
modules.whyItWorks: A business becomes real at the moment money changes hands, and it stays real because of the record sheet. Those five columns tell you next month who your best customers are and whether you are actually making money or just busy. Buying more paper with your own earnings is the moment your shop starts feeding itself.
modules.challenge: Get your first customer to send you your second customer.

words.means: the written line that proves what happened
what is left after you have paid for what you used

courses.title: Your First Company
courses.tagline: By module eight you are not learning about business — you are in one.
courses.intro: You are going to build a small, real, legal business that serves people on your own street and takes in actual money. No pretend shop, no play money. Claude will be your researcher, your drafting assistant and your second pair of eyes — but the customers, the price and the promise are yours.
courses.parentNote: The Claude account is held and opened by you, the parent, teacher or older sibling — Claude's consumer terms are written for adults, so an adult stays alongside while the young person does the thinking and the trading. Modules one and two require no device, the free tier has usage limits that change so check them before each session, and module eight involves handling real money, which is a good moment to agree together on how earnings are split and stored.

modules.title: Twenty Complaints
modules.bigIdea: You do not need a brilliant idea, you need twenty overheard complaints and the patience to sort them.

seeThis.caption: Twenty raw complaints, sorted into piles, leaving three that are worth your time.

doThis: Over three days, collect twenty complaints in the exact words people used. Market, kombi rank, church group, school gate, printing shop queue, your own kitchen.
For each one write three things: who complained, how often it happens to them, and whether it currently costs them money or time.
Sort them into three piles: happens daily, happens weekly, happens rarely. Throw the rare pile away.
From the daily and weekly piles, mark every complaint you could actually help with using only a pencil, a phone and words. Cross out anything needing a machine, a licence or capital you do not have.
You should now have three to five survivors. Write them on a clean page titled MY SHORTLIST and rank them by how much money the complaint currently costs the person.
Read your shortlist to one adult who works for their money. Write down which one they would pay for, and why.
modules.whyItWorks: Most young businesses die because the founder loved the idea and nobody else did. Twenty complaints is a small survey, and a small survey beats a big feeling. Filtering by 'can I do this with words and a pencil' is what keeps a zero-capital business possible at all.
modules.challenge: Find one complaint that at least five different people mentioned independently.

words.means: how many people actually want the thing, not how many say it is nice
the few ideas left after you cut the weak ones

modules.title: Customer, Offer, Price — On Paper
modules.bigIdea: A business is one sentence: I help THIS person do THIS thing for THIS price.

seeThis.caption: Four boxes. If any box is empty, you do not have a business yet.

doThis: Pick the top idea from your shortlist and write the one sentence: 'I help ___ to ___ for ___.' Rewrite it until it fits on one line.
Draw four boxes and fill them. CUSTOMER: exactly who, not 'everyone'. OFFER: exactly what they receive. PRICE: a real number in your currency. COST: what you spend to deliver one.
Work out your margin: price minus cost. Write it big. If it is tiny or negative, change the price or change the offer — do not just hope.
List the three most likely objections a customer will give you: too expensive, I can do it myself, I do not know you. Write one honest answer to each.
Draw a simple poster of your offer by hand — name, what you do, price, how to reach you. This is your first marketing material and it cost nothing.
Show the poster and the one sentence to two adults. Note every question they ask; questions show you what is missing.
modules.whyItWorks: Margin is the whole game. Plenty of busy young sellers work all week and end up with less than they started because the price never covered the cost and their time. Writing customer, offer, price and cost in four boxes forces the arithmetic out into the open before you have promised anything to anyone.
modules.challenge: Say your one sentence to someone in under six seconds and have them understand it.

words.means: the specific thing the customer receives for their money
price minus cost — what is actually left for you
the reason a customer gives for not buying yet

modules.title: Claude as Your Unpaid Assistant
modules.bigIdea: Claude works well when you brief it like a new employee: context, task, format.

seeThis.caption: Three parts in every good prompt. Missing one is why answers come back useless.

youNeed: the adult who holds the account
doThis: Ask the account holder to open Claude and check today's usage limits together — the free tier has limits and they change, so plan a set number of turns before you start.

Write a three-part prompt in your notebook first. Context: 'I am 14, in Kitwe, starting a service that types and prints CVs for people at the market.' Task: 'List the six most common mistakes in a handwritten CV.' Format: 'Six bullet points, under fifteen words each.'
Type it, read the answer, and mark which bullets actually apply to people you know.
Now do it badly on purpose: type just 'CV tips'. Compare the two answers in your notebook and write one sentence on the difference.
Use one turn to have Claude poke holes in your plan: 'Here is my offer and price. What are the three biggest reasons this fails in my town?' Write the three reasons down. Do not argue with them yet.
Answer each of those three reasons in your own words on paper. That page is your plan getting stronger.
modules.whyItWorks: Claude has no idea where you live, what things cost there or who you are unless you say so — it is not hiding that information, it genuinely does not have it. Context, task and format is the briefing a good manager gives, and it is the difference between generic internet advice and something usable at your market on Saturday.
modules.challenge: Get a genuinely useful answer using only one turn, because turns are limited and you are not rich.

words.means: the background facts you give Claude about your real situation
the shape you want the answer in — bullets, a table, five sentences

modules.title: Research It, Then Go And Check It
modules.bigIdea: Claude gives you questions worth asking; the street gives you the answers you can trust.

seeThis.visual: 🤖 says ➡️ 🚶 you walk ➡️ 🗣️ they say ➡️ ✍️ you record
seeThis.caption: The loop that keeps you out of trouble: nothing goes into your plan until a human confirmed it.

doThis: Ask Claude: 'What should I find out about my competitors before starting this service?' Take its list of questions — not its answers about your town, which it cannot know.

Walk out with that list. Visit two people already doing something similar — the printing shop, the older student, the stall next door. Ask politely and write real numbers: what they charge, how long they take, what they refuse to do.
Where Claude guessed a price or a fact about your area, write GUESS next to it. Where a real person told you, write CHECKED. Count both columns.
Find the gap: what do all of them do badly or refuse to do? That gap is where a newcomer with no money can win.
Update your four boxes from module two with the real numbers you collected. Cross out the old ones, do not erase them — you want to see how wrong you were.
Write one paragraph: why a customer would choose me over the two people I visited.
modules.whyItWorks: Claude was trained on text, so it is strong on general patterns and weak on this week's prices at your market. Used correctly it is a question generator and a thinking partner, and the field work stays yours. Mislabelling a guess as a fact is how young businesses set prices that quietly lose money for months.
modules.challenge: Come back with three real prices written in ink and the name of the person who told you each one.

words.means: somebody already selling something like yours
confirm with a real source before you rely on it

modules.title: Draft, Check, Improve — And Say Who Helped
modules.bigIdea: Claude drafts fast, you judge slowly, and the customer is told the truth about both.

seeThis.visual: ✍️ draft ➡️ 🧐 your edit ➡️ 👥 a human reads ➡️ 📤 deliver + 🏷️ 'AI-assisted'
seeThis.caption: Four gates. Nothing reaches a paying customer without passing all four.

doThis: Produce one full sample of your actual service with Claude's help — a tidy CV, a set of birthday card messages, a market price board layout, a WhatsApp broadcast of maize and cassava prices, a study summary sheet.
Edit it hard by hand. Cut anything that sounds foreign to your town, fix names and places, and remove any sentence you could not defend if challenged.
Give it to one honest human to read before any customer sees it. Write down what they stumbled over and fix that.

Ethics moment, write these in your notebook and keep them: I never type another person's private details — ID numbers, medical matters, someone else's phone number — into any AI. I tell customers plainly that AI helped with the drafting. I never submit AI writing as my own schoolwork.
Write the exact sentence you will say to customers, for example: 'I draft this with an AI assistant and then check and finish it myself.' Practise it five times aloud.
File your finished sample in a folder or plastic sleeve. It is your portfolio now.
modules.whyItWorks: Disclosure is not a weakness in a small community — it is why you get sent the next customer. And keeping other people's private details out of any AI tool protects both them and you, especially when the service you sell involves handling someone's documents. A sample checked by a real reader is worth more than ten Claude drafts nobody has seen.
modules.challenge: Find one thing in Claude's draft that is confidently wrong about your area and correct it before anyone else spots it.

words.means: telling people plainly that AI helped
your folder of finished samples that proves you can do the work

modules.title: Price It So It Survives
modules.bigIdea: Set the price from your costs and your time, not from your nerves.

seeThis.visual:
💵 price
− 🧾 cost
− ⏱️ time
= 💰 margin per job
seeThis.caption: One simple sum, written out for one single job, before you sell anything.

doThis: List every real cost for one job: paper, printing shop charge, data bundle, transport, airtime. Add it up honestly, including the small ones.
Time one job with a clock. Multiply by what an hour of your effort is worth to you. Add it to the cost.
Set your price above that total and write the margin per job. If the margin is thin, either raise the price, cut a cost, or offer a smaller version — decide, do not drift.
Build three levels: a small quick version, a standard one, and a bigger one. Most customers pick the middle, and having three makes the middle feel sensible.
Ask Claude to draft your WhatsApp status message and a short price list, then rewrite both in your own voice so they sound like a person your customers know.
Agree with your adult how money will be received — cash in front of them, or into their M-Pesa or EcoCash account — and write that arrangement in your notebook.
modules.whyItWorks: Costs that feel invisible, like a data bundle or the walk to the printing shop, are the ones that eat a young business alive. Writing the sum for one single job makes the margin visible, and three price levels give the customer a choice about size instead of a choice about whether to buy. Some young people running services like this earn a few dollars a week; it is real money, and it grows only if the margin is real.
modules.challenge: Reduce your cost per job by one real item without making the work worse.

words.means: everything you spend to deliver one job
your written levels and prices, so you never invent a number under pressure
paying by phone, for example M-Pesa or EcoCash

modules.title: One Paying Customer
modules.bigIdea: Sell one job, deliver it beautifully, and ask what you got wrong.

seeThis.visual: 🗣️ ask ➡️ 🤝 yes ➡️ 🛠️ deliver ➡️ ❓ 'what would you change?'
seeThis.caption: The whole business, once, at small scale, with one real human.

doThis: Pick the single most likely person from your complaint notebook. Go to them in person, with your sample in your hand.
Show, then ask: 'I do this. It costs [price]. Would you like one?' Then close your mouth and let them answer, however long the silence lasts.
If yes, agree the price, the delivery day and exactly what they get. Write all three in your notebook and read it back to them so there is no argument later.
Deliver early rather than late, and deliver it finished — no 'I will fix that part tomorrow'.
Ask the one question that improves everything: 'What would you change about this?' Write their answer word for word and do not defend yourself.
Ask for one referral: 'Who else do you know who needs this?' Write the name down and go there next.
modules.whyItWorks: The gap between a plan and a business is one person saying yes and handing over money. Delivering early builds the reputation that no advertising can buy in a small community, and the 'what would you change' question gets you honest information that a satisfied nod never will. Referrals are how a zero-capital business grows without spending on marketing.
modules.challenge: Deliver a day earlier than you promised and watch what it does to their face.

words.means: a customer sending you the next customer
handing over the finished work, complete, when you said you would

modules.title: Open For Business
modules.bigIdea: You now trade openly, record every job, and decide on purpose what the profit does next.

seeThis.visual:
DATE | CUSTOMER | JOB | IN | COST | LEFT
12/3 | Baba Musa | 2 CVs | 6 | 2 | 4
seeThis.caption: Your hand-ruled ledger. Six columns, one line per job, no line skipped.

youNeed: adult who holds the account and the mobile money
doThis: Rule your ledger: DATE, CUSTOMER, JOB, MONEY IN, COST, LEFT. Every job gets a line, on the day it happens, even the ones that go badly.
Announce properly: a WhatsApp status and a message to two community or church groups your adult belongs to, with your name, what you do, your prices and how to reach you.
Serve at least three customers this week. Write every line in the ledger as it happens, not from memory on Sunday.
Every evening add up MONEY IN and COST for the day and write LEFT at the bottom. Say the number aloud so it stops being abstract.

At the end of the week split your profit into four named parts and write the amounts in your notebook: restock what you used, save, a share for family or school fees, and a small share for you. Decide the shares before the money arrives, never after.
Look down your ledger and answer two questions in writing: which job type earns me the most per hour, and which customer should I go back to first next week?
modules.whyItWorks: A ledger written on the day is the difference between a business and a hobby that occasionally has money in it. Those six columns let you see which jobs are actually worth your hours and which customer is quietly your best one. Splitting profit into named parts before it arrives is the habit that keeps a small enterprise alive past its first good week.
modules.challenge: Reach ten lines in your ledger, then show it to the adult who opened the account and explain what the numbers are telling you.

words.means: the running written record of money in and money out
what is left after every cost of doing the job is paid
putting some profit back into the business so it can do more
